# The Seventy-Two Hour Court

## I.

They found out about Gerald the way they found out about everything that season—through Mia, who was always first to arrive because her mother dropped her at 5:45 on the way to the hospital's early shift and the school didn't unlock until 6:30, so Mia sat on the curb in the dark eating a granola bar with her gym bag between her knees, waiting. But that Friday she didn't wait on the curb. She called Coach Farrow, and Coach Farrow called the police, and the police called the principal, and the principal sent out the notification at 7:02 a.m., and by the time the rest of the team arrived the gymnasium was wrapped in yellow tape and Gerald Maines, who had managed the equipment for Grover Cleveland High School's athletic department for eleven years, was a shape under a sheet near the storage cage that they could not see but that Mia had already seen and would not describe.

Gerald kept their balls at the right pressure. That was the thing people said later, at the memorial assembly, as though it were a small thing—he kept the balls at the right pressure—but every player who'd ever palmed a game ball knew that Gerald's pressure was different from the pressure of every other ball in every other gym they'd ever played in. He had opinions about it. He had a gauge he'd bought with his own money because the school-issued one was, in his words, "optimistic by two PSI." He called them "my girls" and he didn't mean it in a way that anyone had to think about; he meant it in the way of a man who had something to be custodian of and understood the word the old way, as care, as keeping. He brought fun-size Snickers for the bench during timeouts even though Coach Farrow said sugar was the wrong fuel, and he laid them out on the scorer's table in a line of four, one per player who wasn't in the game, and when Destinee—who sat on the bench more than anyone because she was a junior who'd made varsity on defense alone and her offense was, by her own admission, theoretical—when Destinee took two, Gerald never said a word, just put out five next time. He was fifty-four years old. He had a thermos he brought every day that smelled like soup. He was slight and quiet and had a way of tuning the nets—tightening the loops where they attached to the rim's hooks—that made the swish sound deeper, more certain, a sound like a question being answered. The girls loved him.

The police said it looked like a confrontation near the cage. Blunt force. The cage was where Gerald kept the good balls, the ones with the right pressure, locked up so the general student population couldn't take them for their lunchtime games and return them scuffed and flattened. There was no sign of forced entry at the main doors. The side entrance—the one off the faculty parking lot, the one that required a key card—had been locked when the first-shift custodian scanned in at 5:30.

By noon, they had someone. Dale Kaneck, who had coached Hoover Prep for nine years and been fired six months ago for a recruiting violation that Gerald, of all people, had reported to the district—Gerald, who served on the regional equipment-standards board and had noticed that Hoover Prep was checking out practice gear to kids who weren't enrolled yet, eighth-graders being groomed, brought in for unofficial sessions. Gerald filed the complaint. Kaneck was terminated. And Kaneck, when questioned, did not deny it. He went further than not denying it. He sat in the interview room and said, on camera, "That man took everything from me and I'd do it again," and when the detective asked him to describe what he'd done he described it with the specificity of a man who had been rehearsing the description for months—the weight of the object, the sound Gerald made, the feeling of finally, *finally* being the one who decided how things ended.

Tasha watched the clip on her phone in the parking lot. The team was gathered there because the gym was closed and there was nowhere else to go that was theirs, and they stood in a loose constellation between Mia's mother's parking spot and the chain-link fence, and Tasha held her phone out so they could all see the press conference, the detective confirming the arrest, and behind the detective a glimpse of Kaneck being led out, a man with a windbreaker and the posture of someone who'd been expecting this—not dreading it, expecting it, as though arrest were a form of arrival.

His hatred was real. Anyone could see that. Dale Kaneck had been a man whose identity was coaching, and Gerald's complaint had separated the man from the identity like a shell from a nut, and what was left was soft and pale and furious. He'd been seen at school board meetings in the months after his firing, sitting in the back, not speaking, just watching. He'd sent letters to the local paper that the paper hadn't printed. He'd shown up at Gerald's church once, according to a parishioner, and sat in the last pew and left before communion. He was a man who had lost the thing that organized his days and had replaced it with the person he blamed, and the replacement had structured him just as fully as the coaching had—the surveillance, the obsession, the narrative of injustice he'd built so carefully that confession was not an admission but a culmination. He wanted to be the man who'd killed Gerald Maines. It was the last ambitious thing left to him.

But.

"He's wrong about the door," Tasha said.

No one responded immediately. Mia was crying, had been crying on and off since 5:46 a.m. Destinee had her hand on Mia's back. Aaliyah, the shooting guard, was texting her mother, who'd seen the news and was asking if she was safe.

"He said he came in through the side entrance," Tasha continued, her eyes on her phone, on the clip she'd rewound. "He described propping it open. But the side entrance has been on a thirty-second auto-lock since September. Gerald requested it. Gerald told me—" She stopped. Recalibrated. "Gerald mentioned it. After the booster club people kept leaving it propped for deliveries. He didn't like people having access to the cage. So he put in a work order and they installed the auto-return. Thirty seconds, magnetic. You can't prop it."

Aaliyah looked up from her phone. "So he came in another way."

"Or he didn't come in at all."

Mia wiped her face. Destinee's hand went still on Mia's back.

"He confessed," Destinee said.

"He confessed to a version," Tasha said. "The version's wrong."

Here is what Tasha did next: she put her phone in her jacket pocket and looked at each of them in turn—Mia, Aaliyah, Destinee—and said, "Gerald was ours. If that man didn't do this, then someone else did, and the police aren't even looking because they have what they want. We owe him more than this." Her hands, the narration records, were perfectly steady. Her voice carried the cadence it carried during a fast break, when she called the play and expected execution. She was right about the door and she was probably right about the confession and she was, by any measure, the smartest person in the parking lot, and the certainty she projected landed on the other three like a play being called—a structure they knew how to respond to, roles they knew how to fill.

And Tasha knew—though the other three did not know she knew—that Gerald Maines had spent the last two weeks of his life compiling documentation about her disability classification. The classification that had been filed three years ago, when Tasha was a freshman, by her father's attorney—a specific learning disability designation that reduced her course-load requirements, kept her eligible when her grades in Algebra II threatened to pull her below the 2.0 GPA threshold, and that was, in its clinical specifics, a fabrication. Not entirely. Tasha had been tested. The psychologist her father hired had found what the psychologist was paid to find: a processing deficit that lived in the murky borderland between genuine difficulty and strategic diagnosis, a place where money and a sympathetic evaluator could build a classification that would survive a casual audit but not a determined one. Gerald, with his attention to things that were supposed to be calibrated correctly, had noticed the paperwork in the athletic-academic file during a routine eligibility check—he was meticulous that way, the same instinct that made him distrust the school-issued pressure gauge—and had begun asking questions. Tasha knew this because Gerald, being Gerald, had told her. Had come to her after practice on a Tuesday, thermos in hand, and said, "Tasha, I need to talk to you about your IEP paperwork, because something's not matching up, and I want to give you a chance to look into it before I go to Dr. Robson." Dr. Robson was the principal. Gerald had given her two weeks. The two weeks would have ended Monday.

Tasha looked at her teammates in the parking lot, and her face showed exactly what you'd expect from a captain who had lost someone she cared about and was determined to find the truth, and every part of that was real, and none of it was the whole thing.

"We can figure this out," she said. "We have seventy-two hours before the championship. Let's use them."

---

## II.

Not the gym. The gym was a crime scene and would remain one through the weekend, the yellow tape snapping in the draft from the ventilation system like a pennant for a team no one wanted to play for. Instead, Mia's house—Mia, the center, six-foot-one and still growing, who lived with her mother in a bungalow on Prospect Street where the kitchen table was round and too small for Mia's wingspan and where her mother's nursing textbooks were always stacked on one chair so you had to move them before you could sit, and Mia moved them now, Friday evening, 6:15, setting out glasses of water unasked because that was how Mia operated, anticipating what the body needed before the body knew.

Tasha arrived last, which was unusual. Ordinarily she was first everywhere—first to practice, first to speak, first to see the open lane. She came in with a notebook and a purpose and arranged them at the table according to a geometry only she could see: Mia across from her, Aaliyah to her left, Destinee to her right. She had already divided the work.

"Mia," she said. "You told me once you could lip-read."

"I can follow along if I already know the context," Mia said carefully.

"Thursday afternoon. You were leaving the training room. Gerald was in the office on the phone. You walked past the window."

Mia went still. The glass of water in her hand caught the overhead light.

"You do that thing," Tasha said, not unkindly, "where you watch people's mouths. You told me it started because of your mom's night shifts—you'd FaceTime with the volume off so you wouldn't wake your sister."

"I wasn't trying to—"

"I'm not saying you were. I'm saying you might have seen something that matters. Who was Gerald talking to? What was he saying?"

Mia set the glass down. "I only caught a few words. I wasn't—it was just a second, walking past."

"What words?"

Mia looked at the table. "'Can't keep doing this,'" she said. "'You have to tell them.'" She paused. "'Friday.' He said 'Friday.'"

Tasha wrote this down. Her handwriting was small and angular and she pressed hard enough to leave grooves in the next page.

"Aaliyah. Your mom's at Sisters of Mercy?"

"Intake and triage," Aaliyah said.

"If someone came in Thursday night with an injury—a hand injury, something you'd get from hitting something hard—that record exists."

Aaliyah's composure didn't shift, but a muscle in her jaw tightened by a single degree. "I can't just ask my mother to pull medical records."

"You can ask her to look. That's all. Look."

"That's a HIPAA violation."

"So is murder," Tasha said, which wasn't a legal argument but functioned as one in the room.

Aaliyah said, "I'll ask."

"Destinee."

Destinee, who had been sitting with her hands folded in her lap the way she sat on the bench during games—contained, alert, ready for a role that might not come—looked up.

"The gym is taped but the athletic office isn't. Gerald's desk calendar—the big paper one he kept under his monitor. He wrote everything on it. Meetings, calls, deadlines. It'll have the last two weeks on it. You can get in through the music wing; the connecting door doesn't latch if you push it right."

"How do you know the door doesn't latch?"

"Because I've used it. For extra practice. After hours." This was true. It was not the complete truth.

"So you want me to break into the school."

"I want you to walk into a room that isn't part of the crime scene and bring back a calendar that the police didn't take because they already have a confession and aren't looking."

Destinee said nothing for a moment. Then: "Okay."

"Okay," Tasha repeated, and she drew a line in her notebook under the assignments, and above the line she wrote, in capitals, GERALD, and for a moment they were all looking at his name in her handwriting and the kitchen was quiet and Mia's mother's medical textbooks were stacked on the counter and the refrigerator hummed.

They agreed. They went home. And the omniscient narration, freed from the room's conversational surface, turns now to what each of them carried out the door.

---

Mia drove home—four blocks, she could have walked, but her mother needed the car early and Mia always returned it to the driveway before ten. She parked and sat in the dark with the engine off, hands on the wheel.

She had told the truth about the lip-reading. She had not told the whole truth. She had caught more than a few words through the office window. She'd stopped walking, that Thursday, because Gerald's face had been a face she'd never seen him make—not the gentle logistical calm of the man who tuned their nets, but something compressed and afraid—and she'd stood outside the window for ten seconds, maybe fifteen, and she'd seen enough of his mouth to reconstruct most of his half of the conversation.

*I can't keep doing this. You have to tell them. I'm going to Dr. Robson on Friday. I don't care what it does to the program. This isn't—Coach, this isn't right.*

Coach.

He'd been talking to Coach Farrow. Mia had seen the word form clearly—the *ch* sound pulling his lips, the familiar shape of the name they all said fifty times a practice. And she knew, because she was not stupid and because she occupied the center of the court the way she occupied rooms, taking up space and seeing everything from a height that other people didn't have access to—she knew that something had been wrong between Gerald and Coach Farrow for weeks. Small things. Gerald no longer laid out the Snickers during Coach Farrow's pregame talks; he waited until Coach turned away. Coach Farrow had stopped calling Gerald by name, referring to him instead as "equipment" or "the cage guy," a demotion in language that Gerald had registered—Mia had watched him register it, a flinch around the thermos.

Mia knew what blackmail looked like. Not from experience, but from a childhood that had been organized around her mother's capacity to identify what was wrong with a person from the smallest signs, and Mia had inherited that diagnostic eye. Gerald had something on Coach Farrow. Whatever it was, it had turned their relationship from warmth to formality to something worse, something transactional and strained, and Gerald had reached the end of his willingness to participate in it. *I'm going to Dr. Robson on Friday.*

Friday. Gerald died Thursday night.
